title: Hardwood Floor Transitions and Thresholds: How Pros Handle Doorways and Tile
meta: How pros handle hardwood floor transitions: T-molding, reducers, flush tile edges and doorway breaks for Lynnwood homes. Wills Flooring, $3.25 per sq ft.
keywords: hardwood floor transitions, hardwood to tile transition, T-molding vs reducer, hardwood threshold doorway, flush transition hardwood tile, hardwood floor transition strip
offers: Hardwood floor installation, engineered or solid

blocks.lead: Pros pick the transition by height difference and floor type: a T-molding between two floors at the same height, a reducer down to a lower floor, a flush wood or metal edge against tile, and a threshold to carpet or an exterior door. The piece always sits centered under the closed door.
blocks.detail: The best transition is the one you never notice, and that comes from matching heights before the floor goes down. Installation labor at Wills Flooring is $3.25 per sq ft; transition pieces are material, quoted with your floor.

blocks.html: Lynnwood ramblers and split-levels from the 1960s to 80s are transition-heavy houses: oak under the living room carpet, 1990s tile in the kitchen, sheet vinyl in the laundry, a step down into the family room, a slider to the deck. When the oak gets extended or replaced with new hardwood, every one of those edges has to be resolved. Homeowners ask about the strip. We spend more time on the quarter inch of height it has to hide.

blocks.text: The five pieces and where each belongs

head: Piece
Use it when
What to know
rows: Two hard floors at the same height, or a floating floor that needs an expansion gap in a doorway
Sits in a small channel between the floors. Rocks and cracks if the heights differ by more than about 1/16 in.
Hardwood steps down to a lower floor like vinyl plank or sheet vinyl
Flush reducers are glued or nailed tight and look built-in. Overlap reducers are for floating floors.
Hardwood meets tile at the same height
Either a milled hardwood edge board or a metal profile set in the tile mortar. No lip, no toe-catcher.
Hardwood meets carpet or an exterior door sill
Carpet tucks under the rounded edge. Also covers the gap at sliding-door tracks.
A step down into a sunken room or the top of a staircase
Common in Lynnwood split-levels. Must be solid hardwood, glued and nailed, never a floating piece.
blocks.note: Every piece can be milled from your actual flooring for a perfect match, or bought prefinished in the manufacturer's matching color. We bring both options to the estimate.

blocks.text: Height is the real problem, not the strip

items.text: We measure the finished height of every adjoining floor: tile with mortar, vinyl with underlayment, carpet with pad. Then we pick a hardwood thickness and underlayment that lands within 1/8 in of the neighbor.
A 3/8 in engineered plank next to 3/4 in solid oak gets a layer of plywood underneath. A high side can sometimes be brought down by removing an old underlayment layer.
items.note: Subfloor build-up is quoted at the free estimate; it is the most common hidden line on a transition job.

items.text: Door jambs and casings are cut with a jamb saw so the new floor slides under them. A transition strip should never be notched around trim.

items.d: Set the piece under the door
items.text: The transition is centered under the closed door so each room sees only its own floor. If there is no door, it aligns with the wall face.
Nailed or glued floors get glued and pinned transitions. Floating floors get transitions that clamp without pinning the plank, so the floor can still move.

blocks.text: Doorways: run the boards through or break at the door?

a.title: Best when
items: The same hardwood continues into the next room
The floor is nailed or glued down, so no expansion gap is required at the door
You want the open-plan look Lynnwood buyers expect after a wall comes out
The two rooms will be finished at the same time and with the same finish

b.title: Best when
items: A floating floor exceeds the manufacturer's run length and needs a T-molding gap
The next room gets a different floor, stain or plank direction
The other room will be done later, so a clean edge to pick up from is useful
A closed door separates two rooms that will never be seen together

blocks.text: Hardwood meeting tile: how to get it flush

items.html: Plan the tile height first. Tile plus thinset is usually 1/2 to 5/8 in. If a kitchen is being retiled at the same time, we pick the hardwood thickness and any build-up to land dead level with it.
Choose the edge. A milled hardwood edge board looks warmest and can be sanded later. A slim metal profile set into the tile mortar is cleaner against porcelain and never splits.
Leave a movement joint. Wood moves, tile does not. A flexible color-matched sealant between them, not grout, keeps the joint from cracking every Lynnwood winter.

Watch existing 1990s tile. Many Lynnwood kitchens have tile on a thick mortar bed that sits well above the oak. That usually means a flush reducer milled from the flooring rather than trying to build up a whole room.

blocks.text: Transition mistakes that show up a year later

items.title: Nailing a T-molding through a floating floor
items.text: The pin locks the plank in place, the floor cannot move, and the buckle shows up in the first humid August. Floating floors get clamp-style track transitions only.

items.title: Using a strip to hide a big height gap
items.text: A reducer can handle up to about 1/2 in. Anything bigger is a trip edge and a toe-breaker. The fix is build-up under the low floor, not a taller strip.

items.title: Grabbing the store's stock color
items.text: Prefinished stock transitions rarely match a site-finished or stained floor. Mill them from the same boards, or pick a deliberate contrast, never a near miss.

items.title: Ignoring the step-down room
items.text: Split-level family rooms in Meadowdale and Martha Lake often have a carpeted step down. When the hardwood arrives, that edge needs a real solid stair nose with a return, not a cut-off plank.

blocks.title: One more:
blocks.text: Sliding-door thresholds. The aluminum track on a 1970s slider usually sits above the old floor. New hardwood should meet it with a baby threshold and a bead of exterior sealant. Butting raw wood against the track is how water gets under the first row of boards.

faq.q: What is the difference between a T-molding and a reducer?
faq.a: A T-molding joins two floors at the same height and hides an expansion gap, so it is standard for floating floors in doorways. A reducer slopes down from hardwood to a lower floor such as vinyl plank or sheet vinyl. Use the wrong one and it rocks, cracks or becomes a trip edge.

faq.q: Where should a floor transition go in a doorway?
faq.a: Centered under the door when it is closed. That way each room shows only its own flooring and the door bottom hides the joint. Without a door, the transition aligns with the face of the wall on the side of the room you enter from.

faq.q: Can hardwood meet tile without a transition strip?
faq.a: Yes, if both finish at the same height. We set the tile edge to a straight line, scribe the hardwood to it, and fill the joint with a flexible color-matched sealant instead of grout. The heights have to be planned before either floor goes down.

The pieces are material, quoted with your flooring at the free estimate. Wills Flooring's published installation labor is $3.25 per sq ft for engineered or solid hardwood and covers setting the transitions. Subfloor build-up to match heights is quoted separately once we have measured.

faq.q: Can you run hardwood through a doorway without a break?
faq.a: For nailed or glued hardwood, yes, and it is the cleanest look. Floating engineered floors usually need a T-molding once a run exceeds the manufacturer's length limit, often around 30 to 40 ft, or where the floor changes direction.

faq.q: Why does my old transition strip keep coming loose?
faq.a: Usually because it was nailed into a floating floor or glued over a height gap it could not bridge. As the floor moves, the fastener works loose. The fix is the correct piece for the floor type, set on a level base with the right adhesive or track.
